Front and back

Words, in plain language

Every word the book teaches, in alphabetical order, with the chapter that first explains it. 236 words.

ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVW

A

A/B test
showing a change to a random half of users and comparing them with the other half; the randomising is what lets you say the change caused the difference Chapter 44
AARRR
five stages of growth, each given one countable event: acquisition, activation, retention, referral and revenue Chapter 43
abstention
a system deciding not to answer, and saying so, when it does not have the evidence; it is a product behaviour to be designed, not a sentence in an instruction Chapter 35
acceptance criteria
the teacher's marking rules: the conditions a piece of work must meet to count as done, each written so you can test it Chapter 7
access control
rules that decide which user may see which document or chunk, enforced in the application and data layer, not left to the model Chapter 35
activation moment
the first time a user gets the value the product promises; everything before it is cost to the user Chapter 43
agentic search
a helper who runs several searches by itself, reads what comes back, and rewrites the question, in a loop Chapter 23
AI agent
a helper with a list of errands and a curfew: a model, the functions it may ask for, a loop, and a rule for when to stop Chapter 20
AI value chain
the floors of a building that an AI product stands on: infrastructure, models, tooling and, on top, the apps people use; each floor gets its edge from something different Chapter 31
allowlist
a list of the only things a system is permitted to do; anything not on it is refused Chapter 45
answer key
the teacher's answer key for the guard: for every example sentence, exactly what should be found and what should happen to it, saved in numbered versions Chapter 12
API
an order slip handed across a counter: a way for one program to ask another for something, in a fixed format Chapter 9
API key
a secret password for the model, and it also tells the company whom to bill: a long code that says who is asking; anyone who has it can spend your money Chapter 9
architecture decision record
a short note about a significant technical decision: the alternatives, the choice, the evidence, the consequences, and what would make you revisit it Chapter 40
attack surface
all the places where an outsider can feed something into a system or reach something it can do; every tool, input and connection adds to it Chapter 39
attention
looking back along the sentence: the part of a transformer that works out which other tokens matter most for guessing what comes next Chapter 8
audit trail
a record, kept apart from the work itself, of who did what, when, under which rule and with what result, enough for someone to reconstruct an incident Chapter 39

B

B2B
a shop that sells to other shops. Business to business: a product sold to companies, where the person who pays is often not the person who uses it Chapter 2
B2C
a shop that sells to one person at a time. Business to consumer: a product sold to individual people, who both buy it and use it Chapter 2
bottom-up estimate
like counting the shops in your own lane and adding up what each will pay, instead of taking a slice of a big report; a size you build from customers you can count Chapter 4
bounded agent
an AI agent given hard limits on steps, time and cost, a state it keeps explicitly, and a "cannot resolve" ending, so that it always stops Chapter 36

C

caching
like a shop keeping your usual order ready. The provider remembers the start of a request it has already read. If the start is the same next time, the request is cheaper and faster Chapter 21
canary release
showing a change first to a small share of users, with the old version ready, before everyone gets it Chapter 38
cascade
like a clinic where the nurse sees everyone first and the specialist sees only the hard cases; each request goes to the cheapest step that might work, and only what fails a check moves to a dearer step Chapter 26
case study
a one- or two-page account of a project: the problem and its evidence, your decisions and the options you rejected, the trade-offs, the results with numbers, what failed, and what you would do next Chapter 47
changelog
the short public list of what changed in each release, written for users in practical terms Chapter 46
chunk
like one index card cut from a long book; one piece of a document, small enough to store and send alone Chapter 14
chunking
like cutting a long book into index cards; you choose where each cut goes Chapter 14
claim audit
taking ten claims from an AI-written summary and checking each against its source, marking each supported, partly supported or unsupported Chapter 45
classifier
a sorter with fixed boxes, like the post office sorting letters by pin code: a program that puts each input into one of a fixed set of categories, such as PAN, Aadhaar, mobile number or none of these Chapter 13
code check
a ruler for one thing: a few lines of ordinary code that test one fact about an answer, such as whether a quoted phrase is really in the message; free to run on every change Chapter 25
cohort
a group of users who started in the same period, followed together over time Chapter 44
compaction
making a long chat short. You summarise the middle and keep the beginning and the end Chapter 21
competitor teardown
like laying two phones side by side on a table: for each rival, who it is for, what it costs, where it is good, and what customers complain about Chapter 4
context engineering
packing the model's desk with care. You decide what goes into each request, in what order, and what stays out: the instructions, examples, evidence, chat history and tool results Chapter 21
context judge
a wise elder who reads the tricky sentences: it reads the few sentences the first two parts could not settle and decides if they point to a person Chapter 7
context window
the model's desk: the limit on how much text fits on it at once, counting what you send and what it writes back Chapter 8
contextual retrieval
a note on each index card saying which book and chapter it came from, so a card found alone still makes sense Chapter 23
contribution margin
what a customer leaves you after the costs that grow with them, as a share of what they pay Chapter 42
conversation history
the earlier messages of a chat, like the pages of a ledger; the app must send them again with each new message if it wants the model to seem to remember Chapter 10
cost of delay
like milk going sour on the shelf; what you lose for every week an option waits Chapter 5

D

dark pattern
a design that tricks users into acting against their own interest, such as a pre-ticked box, false scarcity or a hidden cancellation Chapter 43
data contract
the quiet promise between two parts of a system about the data passed along, like "the form will always have a name box"; for example, a field will be there and a list will not be empty Chapter 33
data residency
like the address of the godown where your goods sit; it is the country or region where a provider stores and handles what you send Chapter 28
decision log
a diary for big choices. A page where you write each big decision, the proof for it, and what would make you change your mind Chapter 1
decision memo
like a newspaper story whose first paragraph tells you everything; a short note a busy person can act on after reading its opening Chapter 6
deletion drill
a fire drill for data: pretend a customer asked you to delete their data, then find every place it lives, and see which places you cannot reach Chapter 29
delivery
cooking the dish well in the kitchen. The part of making a product where you build it properly: the plan, the written details, the code and the checking Chapter 2
dependency
like waiting for the plumber before you can paint the wall; anything you need from outside your own team to finish Chapter 6
design partner
an early user who agrees to use an unfinished product and tell you honestly what they find, in return for something fair Chapter 46
diagnosis
like a doctor's finding before any medicine; the first part of a strategy, an honest account of what the real problem is Chapter 5
discovery
finding out what the neighbourhood needs before you open a shop. The part of making a product where you learn if a problem is real and worth solving Chapter 2
distribution
putting the dish on the counter where people can see it. The part of making a product where people find it, try it and keep using it Chapter 2
document audit
like counting what is in a godown before you plan the shelves; you take a random sample and count how much is clean digital text, how much is scanned, and how much hides its meaning in tables and layout Chapter 27
DPDP Act
India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the law that says how to treat people's diaries (personal data); it asks for far more than finding and hiding personal details Chapter 29

E

edge case
an odd parcel at the post office: an unusual input that breaks things the ordinary cases never touch Chapter 7
embedding
an address for meaning; a long list of numbers that puts a piece of text on a map, so texts that mean the same thing live on the same street, even with no shared words Chapter 16
environment variable
a secret kept in a locked drawer outside the code, in the place the program runs; passwords and API keys belong there Chapter 33
error analysis
reading wrong answers one by one and sorting them into piles, like sorting complaints; you read a hundred real outputs, write what went wrong in your own words, group the notes, name the groups and count them Chapter 25
event taxonomy
the list of events a product records, with a naming rule everyone follows, such as object_action in lower case and past tense Chapter 44
evidence pack
the set of things that lets somebody else check your claims instead of just trusting them Chapter 41
exit cost
what it would cost, in money, time and risk, to leave one provider and move to another; a vendor can win on quality and still lock you in for years Chapter 40
experiment runner
a reusable program that writes down every experiment, like a lab notebook: inputs, outputs, settings, timings and errors; it lets you repeat and compare results Chapter 33

F

failure class
a kind of failure, not a single instance of one; it is what makes ten tests meaningful instead of ten stories Chapter 41
failure threshold
the pass mark you write down before the trial starts; if the result falls below it, you call the trial a failure Chapter 32
feasibility
whether the kitchen can really cook the dish. Whether the team can build it with the time, skills, data and money it has Chapter 2
feature flag
a switch in the running system that turns a change on for some users and off for others, without a new release Chapter 45
findings document
a plain, factual record of what broke, the evidence, the root cause, the fix, and what was deliberately left unsolved; the opposite of a brochure Chapter 41
fine-tuning
coaching a model on many examples of your own until it picks up a habit; it teaches behaviour, not facts Chapter 31
five whys
peeling an onion by asking "why?" again and again. You ask it about each answer, to get from a symptom towards its causes Chapter 3
fixed workflow
a sequence of steps decided in advance and written into code, with a model used only for the steps that need judgement Chapter 36
flywheel
a loop in which using the product makes it better, which brings more use; the workflow kind is usually the strongest Chapter 42
Fogg behaviour model
the idea that a behaviour happens when motivation, ability and a prompt meet at the same moment; if it isn't happening, check them in reverse order Chapter 43

G

generative AI
AI that makes new things, such as text, images or code, and does not only give a label or a number Chapter 8
Git
a tool that saves every version of your work, like a photo album of changes, so you can go back to any earlier one Chapter 33
golden dataset
the versioned, representative set of cases, with the behaviour you expect for each, that defines what good means for a system; it has a version number so that a result can be rerun Chapter 38
graceful degradation
when part of a system fails, carrying on in a smaller but safe way instead of failing altogether Chapter 40
gross margin
revenue minus the direct cost of delivering the product; for AI products much of that cost is a model or hosting bill Chapter 42
grounded answer
an answer with its sources attached, like a student who shows which page they copied from. It comes from evidence the system gave, not from what the model happens to remember Chapter 18
growth loop
a cycle in which one user's actions bring in the next user, so that the output feeds back into the input Chapter 43
guardrail metric
like the railing on a bridge; a number that must not get worse while you chase the key results Chapter 6
guiding policy
like the house rules that decide what you will and will not do; the second part of a strategy, your overall approach, including what you refuse Chapter 5

H

hallucination
confident make-believe: an answer that is made up and said with a straight face; it happens because the model guesses likely words, and "I do not know" is rarely the likeliest Chapter 11
harness
everything around the model that makes it a product: the code that builds its context, runs its tools, keeps state, enforces rules, checks quality and records what happened Chapter 45
HTTP
the rules for sending a request and getting a reply, like the rules of posting a letter; each reply has a number that says if it worked Chapter 33
human oversight
a person who can see the proof behind an output and can say no to it; only watching outputs go by does not count Chapter 29
hybrid pricing
a platform fee that includes some usage, then a charge for whatever goes beyond it; predictable for the buyer and protective of your margin Chapter 42
hybrid search
using Ctrl+F style word search and meaning search together, then mixing the two lists, so you do not have to pick one Chapter 23

I

idempotency
the property of an action that can safely be run twice, or is protected so that running it twice has only one effect; it decides whether a retry is safe Chapter 36
incident review
a short written account, made after something goes wrong, of what happened, why, and which check would have caught it Chapter 45
inference
asking the finished model one question: using it to answer a request; it costs money each time and does not change the model Chapter 8
informed consent
a person's agreement, given after being told plainly what is collected, where it goes, what could go wrong and how to withdraw Chapter 46
ingestion
the step of reading documents into a system, including scanning, parsing and splitting them; whatever is lost here is lost for good Chapter 35
input metric
like counting your daily steps to lose weight; a number the team can change directly, which you expect to move the result Chapter 6
instruction tuning
coaching with worked examples: the second stage, where the model learns from instructions paired with good answers, so it follows instructions Chapter 8

J

job to be done
hiring a rickshaw to arrive, not to ride. The progress a person wants to make in their life, which they "hire" a product to help with Chapter 3
JSON
a form written as labels and values inside curly brackets; nearly every API uses it Chapter 9

K

key result
like the marks that show you passed; one of the three or four numbers under a goal. It measures what changed for people, not what you shipped Chapter 6
keyword search
like pressing Ctrl+F; it finds text by matching the exact words of the question, so it compares spelling, not meaning Chapter 15
kill criterion
like a trek rule, "turn back if we have not reached the bridge by noon"; a condition, written in advance, that means you stop the work Chapter 6
kill switch
the main switch on the board: one flag sends traffic to a plain, non-AI path at once, with no new deployment; it works only if that path exists and was tested lately Chapter 30

L

language model
a parrot that has read a whole library: a program that learned from a huge amount of writing to guess what text comes next; it sits behind a chatbot Chapter 8
latency
waiting time, like waiting for your chai after you order; the gap between asking and getting an answer, which users feel as speed Chapter 22
latency budget
the total time a request may take, divided among the stages it passes through, so that the slowest stage is found and has an owner Chapter 40
leaderboard
a school's rank list, but for models; it shows scores on someone else's tests, not yours Chapter 34
leading question
a question that nudges the answer, like "this is very fresh, isn't it?" It suggests the answer the asker is hoping for Chapter 3
least privilege
giving a system only the access it really needs, so that if it is fooled the damage stays small Chapter 39
lethal trifecta
three things that together make a system dangerous: it can see private data, it reads text that outsiders can write, and it has a way to send something out Chapter 24
LLM judge
a second student marking the homework; a model that grades another model's answers, cheap and fast, but it has biases, so check the marker against the teacher before you trust it Chapter 25
lock-in
being stuck with one provider because leaving costs too much, in rewriting, remeasuring or lost features Chapter 31

M

mask
to hide part of a detail but keep its shape, for example 98******12 Chapter 7
MCP
Model Context Protocol: a standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data, so that any compliant tool fits any compliant application, like a plug and a socket Chapter 36
metadata filtering
labels on every file, such as version, dates and who may see it; you throw out the files that cannot be right before any scoring Chapter 23
minimum detectable effect
the smallest change worth detecting; it sets how many users a test needs Chapter 44
model selection card
a one-page file card for the choice: the task, the quality target, the limits on data, speed and cost, the options tried, the evidence and the fallback; it shows a reviewer why you chose that model Chapter 34
MoSCoW
like packing a bag for a trip, sorting things into Must, Should, Could and Won't take Chapter 5
multimodal
able to take in more than text, such as pages, pictures, tables and speech, which changes what counts as evidence and how it is traced Chapter 37
must-keep list
the facts a reader must not lose, written down for each document; every summary is ticked against it, like a shopping list Chapter 13
MVP
minimum viable product, the smallest thing that tests your riskiest guess with real users Chapter 7

N

name-and-place finder
a guard who reads names on a list: it finds details with no fixed shape, such as a person's name, an address or an employer Chapter 7
network effect
the product getting better for everyone as more people use it, which is not the same as users bringing in other users Chapter 43
North Star
like the star sailors steer by; one sentence about what your customers gain, and one number that measures it Chapter 5

O

observability
being able to see, from the records a system keeps, what it did and why, without guessing Chapter 38
observation session
a meeting in which you give someone a real task and watch them do it without helping, noting the same things each time Chapter 46
OCR
like a clerk who reads a photo aloud and types what they hear; optical character recognition is software that turns a picture of text into text, usually with a few mistakes Chapter 27
OKR
like a report card goal with marks beside it: objectives and key results, a goal in words with a few numbers that show you reached it Chapter 6
open-weight model
a recipe published for everyone: you can download the model (its weights) and run it on your own computers, instead of calling someone else's Chapter 31
opportunity tree
like a family tree for ideas: it starts at the result you want, grows branches for the needs people told you about, and ends in possible fixes Chapter 4
orphaned chunk
like a page torn from a letter; it points to something that was in the piece before, so alone it makes no sense Chapter 14
outcome pricing
charging for each successful result, so that the price follows the value; it needs an agreed, measurable definition of success Chapter 42

P

p95
the time that 95 out of 100 requests beat; it shows the slow tail that an average hides Chapter 38
parser
the program that turns a file such as a PDF into text and structure; its mistakes are invisible to everything that comes after it Chapter 35
pattern checker
a guard at a gate who checks tickets by their look: it finds details that always have the same shape, such as a PAN or a mobile number, using fixed rules Chapter 7
persona
a passport page for one kind of user. A short description of one type of user, built only from what interviews showed Chapter 3
PII
someone's diary page. Any detail that can point to one real person, such as a name, a phone number or an identity number Chapter 1
pilot
a small trial run, like a trial batch before cooking for the whole wedding; it shows if a feature helps the business, and says in advance what result means failure Chapter 32
pinned version
a model version fixed by its exact name, so the provider cannot swap it under you without telling you Chapter 30
positioning statement
like the one line on a shop board that says who the shop is for and why it is different; one sentence about your product Chapter 4
PRD
product requirements document, the recipe card for a dish: it says what to build and why, starting from the problem and its evidence Chapter 7
pre-mortem
like tasting the dish in your head and finding it burnt before you cook; a meeting where everyone supposes the project has failed and writes down why Chapter 6
pre-training
school years in a huge library: the first and most costly stage of making a model, where it learns to guess the next token across a vast amount of text Chapter 8
precision
like checking the net for real fish; of everything the tool flagged, the share that really was what it claimed. If it flagged 100 and 80 were real, precision is 80 percent Chapter 17
predictive AI
AI that gives one label or one number for one job, such as whether a message is spam Chapter 8
problem statement
one short note saying who is hurt, how, and what it costs them today. It is one or two sentences Chapter 3
product risk
one leg of a four-legged table. Break one leg and the table falls. It is one of four things that can sink a product: nobody wants it, nobody can use it, it cannot be built, or it cannot pay for itself Chapter 2
product sense
the ability to choose a user, find their real problem and propose a sensible solution, which interviewers test with questions such as "design a voice assistant for a state helpline" Chapter 47
product-led growth
winning customers by letting users sign up and get value on their own, with some of them upgrading; it fits when the value shows in minutes and the price is low Chapter 43
production delta
the list of everything missing between a working prototype and a running service, such as identity, retries, queues, monitoring, secrets, backups and rollback Chapter 40
project memory
a plain file kept with the code, holding the rules and habits of the project, loaded at the start of every run of a coding assistant Chapter 45
prompt
the note you hand the model: what you want, and how; it can hold instructions, examples and the material to work on Chapter 11
prompt injection
a hidden note inside a letter you were asked to read, that says "ignore your teacher"; text in material the model only had to read gives it orders, and the model may obey because it cannot reliably tell your orders from words it was asked to read Chapter 24
prototype
a cardboard toy house: a rough, cheap version made to learn something before the real one exists Chapter 7
provenance
the paper trail that says where something came from, so you can trace a claim or a decision to its source, its version and the code that made it Chapter 34
Python
the programming language most AI work is written in; for a product manager, a way to say exactly what an experiment does Chapter 9

Q

quasi-identifier
a clue that is harmless alone but can point to one person when added to others, such as age, village and a rare illness Chapter 7

R

reasoning model
a student who works on rough paper before writing the answer; the model tries a way, checks it, then replies, and you pay for that rough work on every request, in money and in waiting time Chapter 22
recall
like the fish in a net; of all the real items there were to find, the share the tool found. If there were 100 and it found 90, recall is 90 percent Chapter 17
red team
people whose job is to attack a system on purpose, so that they find its weaknesses before anyone else does Chapter 39
redact
to remove a detail completely, for example by replacing it with the word [PAN] Chapter 7
refusal
a polite "no" from the tool, like a shopkeeper saying "not here, go to that counter"; it says plainly it cannot do the task and points to a person; you design it on purpose Chapter 32
regression
a change that makes a system worse at something it used to do well Chapter 38
release gate
an automatic check that runs the golden dataset against a change and blocks the release if any number falls below its threshold Chapter 38
repository
a cupboard that keeps every old copy of your notes. An online folder, on a site such as GitHub, that keeps a project's work and every older version Chapter 1
reranking
a quick helper pulls a big pile of pages, then a slower, careful reader reads the question and each page together and puts the best few on top Chapter 23
residual risk
the risk that is left after the controls are in place; it should be written down, not assumed away Chapter 39
retention
like a shopkeeper who keeps your bill copy for a month after you leave; it is how long a provider keeps what you send, often far longer than the time it takes to answer Chapter 28
retrieval
the finding step, like pulling the right page out of a file. The system looks through your documents for the pieces that fit the question Chapter 18
retrieval-augmented generation
RAG: an open-book exam for the model. First the system finds the pages that look right for the question. Then it hands those pages to the model with the question, and the model writes its answer from them Chapter 18
RICE
like marks in an exam: a score for each option, Reach times Impact times Confidence, divided by Effort Chapter 5
risk register
a table that lists each risk with its owner, its control, the evidence that the control works, and what risk remains Chapter 39
risk tier
a speed limit for a system: the more harm a wrong answer can do, the more documents, checks and proof it needs; the use sets the tier, not the technology Chapter 29
riskiest assumption
the weakest plank in a bridge. The thing that must be true for your idea to work, and that you are least sure of, so you test it first Chapter 3
roadmap
like a family's plan for the week: tonight is fixed, next week is likely, someday is a wish; it shows what a team will work on and roughly when, in three columns, Now, Next and Later, with results promised instead of dates Chapter 6
role matrix
a table with the skills that real job advertisements ask for down one side and the roles across the top, in which you mark each skill as proven, partly proven or missing for yourself Chapter 47
rollback
going back to the old version of the code, like swapping back to last year's recipe; it needs a new deployment, and it does not help when both versions share the same bad behaviour Chapter 30
rollback trigger
a measurable condition, written down beforehand, that obliges someone to undo a release Chapter 45
routing
a front desk that sends easy requests to the cheap helper and only the hard ones to the dear expert; each request goes to the cheapest model that can handle it Chapter 34
rule-keeper
the clerk with the rule book: it decides what to do with each detail found, such as remove it, mask it, let it through or ask Chapter 7

S

SAM
serviceable addressable market: like the shops in your part of the city that you can really reach with what you have; the part of the TAM you could serve Chapter 4
schema
the blank form itself: it lists every box, what goes in it, and which boxes must be filled. The company running the model enforces it while the model writes Chapter 19
scoreboard
the table that counts, for each version of the tool, what it found, what it missed and what it wrongly flagged Chapter 12
SDK
software development kit: a small library plus a demo that another developer can add to their own product without building the feature themselves Chapter 41
seat pricing
charging for each user of the product, per month; easy for a buyer to budget, but unfair when heavy users cost far more to serve than light ones Chapter 42
shadow AI
staff quietly using free consumer AI tools, often by pasting in office documents, because those tools help and nothing approved is as good Chapter 29
similarity score
like a marks card for closeness; a number from about 0 to 1 that says how near two embeddings are, and it means little until you know what clearly good and clearly bad matches score Chapter 16
SOM
serviceable obtainable market: like the shops you could really win in about three years; the part of the SAM you could actually get Chapter 4
speaker attribution
working out who said which words in a recording; it looks technical and behaves like a privacy decision Chapter 37
speech-to-text
software that turns recorded speech into written words; it is the first stage of any voice system and the first place where meaning can be lost Chapter 37
sprint
a fixed stretch of one or two weeks in which a team plans, builds, shows and reviews its work Chapter 7
staging
a copy of the live system where changes are tried first, so that a bad change never reaches real users Chapter 40
stakeholder
like the people at a wedding who can make it work or stop it, such as the cook and the hall owner; anyone who can help or stop a project, or is affected by it Chapter 6
STAR method
a way to tell a story about your own past in four parts: situation, task, action and result, with most of the time spent on what you did Chapter 47
state machine
a workflow in which your code fixes every step and every allowed move from one step to the next Chapter 45
stateless
forgetful, like a goldfish: it keeps nothing between requests, so every call starts from nothing and the model does not know you spoke a moment ago Chapter 10
status code
the number on an HTTP reply, like a marks slip: 200 means it worked, 4xx means your request was wrong, 5xx means the other side failed Chapter 33
status quo
like the old habit at home that everyone keeps because it works a little; what people do today, even if that is nothing. It is usually the strongest rival Chapter 4
step limit
the curfew. The most rounds an AI agent may take before it must stop. The program sets it, never the model Chapter 20
streaming
the chai-wala saying "two minutes" while he works; the answer reaches the screen a few words at a time as it is written, not all at the end Chapter 22
structured output
a form with fixed boxes. The model fills named boxes of a known type, so a program can read them, instead of writing a paragraph for a person Chapter 19
sub-agent
a helper given one part of a large task, which works in its own separate context so that the main one stays small Chapter 45
support log
a running record of every request for help, with its category and the account it came from, read weekly as evidence about the product Chapter 46
system card
a one-page label for an AI system, like the label on a medicine strip: what it is for, what data it uses, how it was tested, what it gets wrong and what it must not be used for Chapter 29
system prompt
the standing instructions on the shop wall, read before every order; the app sends them with every request to say who the assistant is and what it must and must not do Chapter 11
system-design interview
a conversation in which you are asked to design an AI feature aloud, and judged on your reasoning about approach, evaluation, failure, cost and rollout, not on code Chapter 47

T

take-home
a piece of work set by an employer to be done alone within a time limit, which tests how you work when no one is watching Chapter 47
TAM
total addressable market: like every shop in the whole city that could ever want your product, at your price; everyone who has the problem Chapter 4
task type
which of five kinds of job a request really is: classify, extract, summarise, rewrite or generate Chapter 12
temperature
a dial for how adventurous the model is with its next word; low plays safe and gives similar answers each time, high takes chances and gives more variety Chapter 11
test set
the teacher's question paper, with the right answers written down beforehand: real or realistic examples used to measure a system Chapter 12
time-box
a fixed amount of time for unsure work, with a decision at the end of it Chapter 7
time-to-value
how long a new user takes to reach the activation moment, measured from sign-up Chapter 43
token
one Lego brick of text: a piece of text, often a whole word and sometimes part of one; models read in bricks, and providers charge per brick Chapter 8
token budget
a shopping budget for bricks of text. A plan that gives each part of a request its share of tokens, with one person who owns the total and knows what to cut first Chapter 21
tool calling
the model asks a shopkeeper to check the stock. The model names a function and what to give it, and your program runs it and sends back the result Chapter 20
tool contract
the precise written agreement for one function a model may call: its name, what it does and does not do, its parameters, its errors, its side effects and who is allowed to call it Chapter 36
tool description
the label on a shop shelf. A few lines that tell the model what a function does, what it gives back and what it does not. The model picks by reading the label, so a vague label is a bug Chapter 20
toolchain
the set of tools a team uses to build and run a product, thought of as slots to be filled, each with a job to do Chapter 45
trace record
the saved record of one request's whole path through the system: the input, the versions, the steps, the timings, the cost and how it ended Chapter 38
tracking plan
the shared document that lists every event, its properties, when it fires and who owns it, which engineers build from and analysts trust Chapter 44
transformer
the design almost every modern language model is built on; its key part is attention Chapter 8

U

usability
a door you can open without a sign. Whether people can work out how to use something without help Chapter 2
usability test
watching a real person try a task with a prototype, without helping them Chapter 7
usage block
the bill that comes with each reply: how many tokens went in and how many came out, which is what you are charged for Chapter 9
usage pricing
charging for each unit used, such as each message or call, so that revenue follows cost; buyers can't predict the bill and may ration their use Chapter 42
user interview
a witness giving a statement, not a vote. A talk to learn what a person really did and needed, not whether they would like your idea Chapter 3
user story
one piece of value told from the user's side: who they are, what they want, and why Chapter 7

V

validation
the second check after the answer arrives, like a clerk checking your filled form. Is every box filled? Does each quoted phrase really appear in the message? Chapter 19
value proposition
like the board outside a shop; a plain statement of who you serve, what job you do for them, and why you are better than what they have now Chapter 5
verifier
a check, such as a test, that tells an agent whether its own change worked, without a person reading every line Chapter 45
vertical slice
a thin cycle that already rolls: a working version that goes through every layer of the system, so a real user can try it early Chapter 7
viability
whether the shop earns more than it spends. Whether the product works for the business: its income, its costs, the law and its good name Chapter 2
virality
users bringing in other users Chapter 43
voice pipeline
the chain of separate stages a voice system runs through, from capturing the sound to acting on it, each adding delay and each able to change the meaning Chapter 37

W

wedge
like the thin end of a wedge that goes into a log first; the small first use you can clearly win, which opens the way to something bigger Chapter 5
weights
the dials inside the model: billions of numbers that hold everything it has learned; training turns them and everyday use does not Chapter 8
worked example
a finished sample of the output you want, shown to the model so it copies the format instead of guessing from your description Chapter 11
